title: The Afternoon Brief: Tennis in the early hours; football's legal wars escalate
dek: Ben Shelton defeated Carlos Alcaraz at 3:34 a.m. ET in the latest US Open finish ever, guaranteeing an all-American men's semifinal. Meanwhile, the SEC scheduled Thursday's expulsion vote on LSU, the CFP opened playoff expansion talks with ESPN, and LIV Golf's Chapter 11 filing revealed hundreds of millions in unresolved player and vendor claims.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Wednesday's stories map a sports landscape where governance structures are being tested: conferences testing expulsion power, tours restructuring under court supervision, and playoff formats undergoing formal renegotiation, all while athletes from tennis to football navigate the uncertain terrain these institutional shifts create.
bottom_line: The SEC's Thursday vote, LIV's court proceedings, the CFP's December 1 deadline, and the federal lawsuit over LSU's status all hinge on whether governance bodies can enforce rules they have rarely tested. Shelton and Tiafoe's all-American semifinal offers a counterpoint: a sports outcome determined by play, not procedure. The coming 72 hours will reveal whether the SEC can assemble expulsion votes, whether BC Partners' restructuring gains court approval, and whether the CFP and ESPN can reach alignment on playoff expansion before the calendar forces a decision.
body: Three institutional crises advanced today while two tennis players made history in the early morning hours. The through-line is governance under strain: conferences and leagues testing enforcement authority they have rarely or never exercised, restructuring under duress, and the calendar tightening on decisions that reshape who competes where.

Ben Shelton defeated defending US Open champion Carlos Alcaraz 6-7 (5-7), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) in a five-set quarterfinal that ended at 3:34 a.m. ET, the latest finish in US Open history according to BBC Sport. The match lasted 4 hours and 28 minutes. Shelton's victory over world No. 3 Alcaraz marked his first win over a top-three player in 17 attempts and guarantees an American finalist for the first time since 2003, per BBC Sport. Moments earlier, Frances Tiafoe defeated Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6) in a quarterfinal lasting 4 hours and 38 minutes, completing the first two-set-down comeback in a US Open men's quarterfinal since Roger Federer's victory over Gael Monfils in 2014, per ESPN. Both Americans now meet in Friday's semifinal, ensuring at least one American reaches Sunday's final for the first time in 23 years.

The SEC filed an amended federal complaint Tuesday seeking legal authority to expel LSU from the conference and scheduled a vote by conference presidents for Thursday, September 10. The filing adds members of LSU's Board of Supervisors and Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill as defendants. SEC bylaws require a two-thirds majority of conference presidents to vote for expulsion. The central dispute involves LSU's recruitment and rostering of players who held NFL contracts, specifically tight end Dae'Quan Wright and defensive lineman Zxavian Harris, both of whom LSU did not roster for the season opener against Clemson. Wright had signed with the Eagles before being cut and then signed with the Browns; Harris signed with the Saints and was cut in August. Both said they could earn six figures playing for LSU this fall, per Front Office Sports. The SEC's amended complaint alleges the school "waged a deliberate, coordinated, and public campaign to recruit professional athletes," mentioning head coach Lane Kiffin 32 times across 44 pages. Kiffin has denied the allegation. In the SEC's 94-year history, only one power conference has voted to expel a member: the Big East expelled Temple following the 2004 season. Multiple sources told CBS Sports they believe the league has the necessary votes if LSU refuses to de-escalate. However, a Louisiana state court has already issued a preliminary injunction clearing the way for the players to compete, creating a potential conflict between state and conference authority.

LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court of New Jersey on September 8, 2026, with BC Partners Credit backing a restructuring agreement. The filing estimates liabilities between $500 million and $1 billion against assets valued at $100 million to $500 million. The Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) ended its funding in April 2026 and has committed $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession financing to cover operations during restructuring, an amount covering less than 10 percent of estimated liabilities. The unsecured player creditors list is led by Jon Rahm, followed by Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson, each with claims exceeding $5 million. IMG Media is owed the largest single amount among non-player creditors at $3.2 million. Rahm separately is reported to be owed more than $100 million from his multiyear contract signed before the 2024 season. LIV intends to resume competition in 2027 under a player-majority ownership model with field sizes expanding to 75 players per event and Monday qualifiers introduced, though no definitive 2027 schedule has been announced. BBC Sport reports that contracts under the previous LIV Golf iteration will terminate because of the court filing, and no obligation exists for players to sign with a restructured LIV 2.0 regardless of previous agreements. The restructuring deal has not closed and requires court and stakeholder approval.

The College Football Playoff triggered a mandatory 30-day negotiating window with ESPN on Tuesday, September 8, beginning formal discussions on expanding the playoff to 24 teams in 2027. The CFP's statement tempered expectations: "This does not represent a decision or commitment to expand, but rather an opportunity to engage with ESPN and gather additional information to help determine a path forward." The window gives ESPN and the CFP until December 1 to reach agreement on revised media rights. On that same date, conferences must notify their broadcast partners whether they intend to drop conference championship games. The move signals serious exploration of expansion, though expansion would eliminate conference championships, reshape the bowl schedule, and require ESPN to account for the loss of at least $200 million in annual media value from those games, per ESPN's reporting.

In other contract news, Baker Mayfield signed a three-year, $165 million extension with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on September 8, locking him through the 2029 season at an average of $55 million per year. The extension is the largest in Buccaneers franchise history. Mayfield sought a longer commitment than the two-year offer Tampa Bay initially proposed during a training-camp holdout that ended over the weekend. At $55 million per year, Mayfield joins an elite quarterback salary tier alongside Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love, per ESPN. ESPN's Ben Solak graded the deal a B, noting Mayfield has "high peaks" but must now deliver "high-level, veteran consistency" to return value on the extension. The Buccaneers' roster has undergone turnover: they missed the playoffs for the first time since 2020 last year, wide receiver Mike Evans has departed, and linebacker Lavonte David is no longer on the roster.
